t: Maximum Sum of Subsequence With Non-adjacent Elements
o:
## Understanding the problem

We maintain an array under point updates; after each update we must report the classic house-robber answer: the maximum sum of a subsequence with no two chosen elements adjacent (empty subsequence allowed, so the answer is never negative). We return the sum of all query answers modulo 1e9+7.

Example 1: `[3,5,9]` → after `nums[1]=-2`, best is `3+9=12`; after `nums[0]=-3`, best is `9`; total 21.

With n, q up to 5·10⁴, recomputing an O(n) DP per query is 2.5·10⁹ operations — too slow. We need a structure supporting point update and full-array DP query in O(log n): a segment tree where each node summarizes the robber DP for its segment.
k: Each segment tree node stores a 2×2 matrix M[l][r] = best sum using the segment where we record whether the first (leftmost) and last (rightmost) elements are taken.
Merging child L and R: combining left-taken state of L with left-taken state of R is forbidden (they are adjacent across the boundary).
Since the empty subsequence is allowed, clamp leaf values with max(v, 0) for the 'nothing taken on this side' state; the root's M[0][0] is the answer.

a.n: Approach 1: Segment tree of 2×2 DP states
a.i: The robber DP is associative: knowing, for each segment, the four values 'best sum given whether boundary elements are used' lets us merge two segments in O(1) by trying all compatible state combinations. Point updates touch O(log n) nodes, and each query is just reading the root — perfect for interleaved updates and whole-array queries.
s: Leaf for value v: `M[0][0]=max(v,0)` (skip it), `M[1][1]=v` (take it), off-diagonal = −∞ (can't take the same element as both boundaries).
Merge(L,R): `res[l][r] = max(L[l][0]+R[0][r], L[l][1]+R[1][r])` for all l,r ∈ {0,1} — the forbidden adjacency (L takes its right, R takes its left) never appears.
On each query, point-update the leaf, pull up ancestors, add root M[0][0] to the answer modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) — each update rebuilds one root-to-leaf path.
a.sp: O(n) for the segment tree arrays.

w:
## Wrap-up

This is the canonical 'DP over segments' segment tree (same family as GCD-with-update and matrix-product trees). Pitfalls: forgetting the empty-subsequence clamp (negative arrays would give negative answers), accidentally allowing the cross-boundary adjacency in the merge, and skipping the modulo on partial sums. Follow-ups: range queries of the robber value instead of the whole array (same node structure, descend the tree), or adding lazy reversals.
